$comment: The repertoire, as branches to crawl. This is the machine-readable form of
docs/repertoire-v1.md — that file says why these openings and not others;
this one says where each crawl starts. Change them together.
A forced `line` pins the OPENING CHOICE and stops. Everything past it is the
generator's job: which deviations to cover, how deep, and where the line goes
quiet. Forcing a whole main line would make this a memorisation deck with extra
Branches nest. A sweeper such as `d4 d5 c4` covers the rare replies and hands
each named branch its own subtree; build.mjs derives the boundaries and
refuses to run if any of them leaves a gap. See src/domain/repertoirePlan.ts.

entries.name: 1.d4 — irregular replies
entries.why: Everything that is not 1...d5, 1...Nf6, 1...f5 or 1...e5. Mostly move-order tries that transpose; the point is not to be surprised.
entries.$roleNote: Covers the replies no curated branch owns. The value is meeting 1...c5 or 1...g6 at all, not five moves of follow-up — at full depth this one branch cost 70 of the repertoire's 467 decisions.
entries.$coverageNote: v1 shipped on the defaults and quietly covered only six replies, of which four (1...d5, 1...Nf6, 1...f5, 1...e5) it hands straight to curated branches. 1...c5 ranks seventh, so the moves this branch *exists* for fell off the end: 11% of the owner's real games as White reached a position with no answer. The mass after 1.d4 is dominated by the replies we delegate, which is exactly the case `massTarget`'s doc comment warns about.

entries.name: Queen's Gambit — rare 2nd moves
entries.why: The tail after 2.c4: early bishop sorties and pawn moves. Two of the repertoire's confirmed traps live here, both punished the same way — take on d5 and hit b7.

entries.name: QGD Exchange — the Carlsbad
entries.why: One structure, one plan: the minority attack with b4-b5. The best understanding-per-unit-theory in the repertoire, which is why the Exchange rather than the main line.

entries.name: QGA — do not chase the pawn
entries.why: The priority line. White does not rush to regain c4; develop and let the attempt to HOLD the pawn cost Black the position. The break to know is a4 against ...b5.
entries.$depthNote: Set against the depth floor: the punishing line 3.e3 b5 4.a4 c6 5.axb5 cxb5 6.Qf3 lands on ply 11, so the cap must clear it. If minPly ever rises past 11 this branch can no longer reach its own priority line.

entries.name: Slav — the White side
entries.why: The same structure we play as Black. Learning it from both sides is the point of pairing the Queen's Gambit with the Slav.

entries.name: Albin Counter-Gambit
entries.why: Common at this band and objectively bad, which is exactly the combination worth an evening. Note the trap here is OURS to avoid: 4.e3?? Bb4+ is the Lasker Trap, and the generator will not show it because it only ever picks sound moves for us.

entries.name: Marshall Defence
entries.why: Refuted by taking the centre. A clean illustration that a developing move can be a mistake if it ignores the middle of the board.

entries.name: Chigorin Defence
entries.why: Sideline coverage. Black gives up the centre for piece play; we are happy to take it.

entries.name: 1...Nf6 2.c4 — the rest
entries.why: Benoni, ...c6 and ...b6 move orders. Where theory explodes, so depth here is set by measured frequency, not ambition.

entries.name: 1...Nf6 2.c4 e6 — Nimzo/QGD complex
entries.why: Plan level only. Many of these transpose straight back into the Queen's Gambit lines above.

entries.name: 1...Nf6 2.c4 g6 — King's Indian / Grünfeld
entries.why: Plan level only. Two completely different games depending on whether Black plays ...d6 or ...d5; knowing which one you are in is most of the battle.

entries.name: Budapest Gambit
entries.why: Common here, and carries a smothered-mate trap for the greedy White player. Worth knowing from the side that is supposed to be better.

entries.name: Dutch Defence
entries.why: Sideline coverage. Fianchetto and take the long diagonal; the h1-a8 diagonal is what 1...f5 gave away.

entries.name: Englund Gambit
entries.why: Objectively junk that scores absurdly well below 1600 — the definition of a line worth preparing. Take the pawn and keep it.

entries.name: Caro-Kann — White's 2nd move
entries.why: Everything except 2.d4: the two-knights, 2.c4, 2.Nf3 and the pass moves. Mostly transpositions back into the main structures.
entries.$roleNote: White's alternatives to 2.d4. Meeting them is the point; the structures that follow are taught by the curated Caro branches.

entries.name: Caro-Kann — 2.d4 d5, White's 3rd move
entries.why: The junction of the whole defence. White must now commit: push, take, or defend e4. The three main answers each get their own branch; this covers the rest (3.Nd2, 3.f3, 3.Be3).
entries.$massNote: 3.Nc3, 3.e5 and 3.exd5 are exactly 85% of this node, so the default coverage target is met before a single move this branch owns is reached — and it covers nothing. Raised so the tail it exists for gets in.

entries.name: Caro-Kann Classical — 3.Nc3 dxe4
entries.line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4
entries.why: The Classical, heading for ...Bf5 — the problem bishop gets outside the pawn chain before ...e6 shuts it in. Learning THIS rather than 4...Nd7 also sidesteps 5.Qe2 Ngf6?? 6.Nd6#, which is the one Caro-Kann trap everyone falls for once.

entries.name: Caro-Kann Advance — 3.e5 Bf5
entries.line: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5
entries.why: A French structure with the good bishop already outside — the entire point of playing 1...c6 rather than 1...e6.

entries.name: Caro-Kann Exchange and Panov — 3.exd5 cxd5
entries.line: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5
entries.why: White chooses between the quiet Exchange (4.Bd3) and the Panov (4.c4), which hands us an IQP position — the same structure the Queen's Gambit gives us from the other side.

entries.name: 1.d4 d5 — White's 2nd move
entries.why: The London, Jobava and Colle setups, which appear constantly at this band and are played almost regardless of what we do. Plans, not theory.
entries.$roleNote: The London, Jobava and Colle are plans played almost regardless of what we do, and this file says plans, not theory. At full depth it cost 69 decisions for setups that need one good answer.

entries.name: Slav — White's 3rd move
entries.why: The c6-d5 chain, the same one the Caro-Kann builds. One structural idea covers the entire Black repertoire.

entries.name: Slav main line — 3.Nf3 Nf6
entries.line: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6
entries.why: Where ...dxc4 followed by ...Bf5 becomes available: the resource that makes the Slav more than a passive defence.

entries.name: Exchange Slav — 3.cxd5 cxd5
entries.line: d4 d5 c4 c6 cxd5 cxd5
entries.why: Appears constantly and is far less drawish than its reputation below master level. Symmetry is not equality; the half-open c-file is the whole game.

entries.name: 1.c4 — into Slav structures
entries.why: Steer toward the same c6-d5 chain rather than learning a separate anti-English system.
entries.$roleNote: The decision is 1...c6. After it we are in Slav structures the curated branches already cover, so depth here buys the same positions twice.

entries.name: 1.Nf3 — into Slav structures
entries.why: Same idea: take the centre and transpose into what we already know.
entries.$roleNote: The decision is 1...d5. Same reasoning as the English — 48 decisions at full depth for a transposition we already know.

entries.name: Irregular first moves
entries.why: 1.Nc3, 1.b3, 1.f4 and 1.g3. Rare individually, but v1 answered none of them, and 2% of games is one board in a five-round tournament. Take the centre and steer toward the same c6-d5 chain the rest of the repertoire teaches.
entries.$roleNote: Rooted at the initial position — the only branch that is — so it catches whatever the four real Black branches do not own. It delegates 1.e4, 1.d4, 1.c4 and 1.Nf3 on the very first ply, which is what makes the breadth affordable.
